title: nvidia-persistenced and cgroup v2: runtime-induced latency variance across A100/H100/L40S SKUs
content:
Goal:
Quick investigation notes: how system-level GPU daemon (nvidia-persistenced) + cgroup v2 tuning (cpu/memory io throttles, cpuset) interact with per-request P50/P95/P99 latency on different cloud SKUs (A100 / H100 / L40S) and different NVIDIA driver + CUDA stacks. We suspect intermittent tail amplification in small-batch (1-4 token start) workloads is triggered by daemon wakeups and cgroup reclaim events, which show up as 1-20ms spikes that cascade into decode tail latency under high request churn.

Summary findings (high level):
- Turning off nvidia-persistenced in our AMI/images reduces sporadic 5-15ms latency spikes for small requests on A100 in AWS p4d-like instances; effect less pronounced on H100 instances tested on GCP.
- cgroup v2 memory.high and io.max settings we applied to containers can cause kernel reclaim activity when memory pressure is near threshold; that reclaim correlates with p95/p99 tail spikes during kv-cache repopulation. L40S instances exhibited higher sensitivity (likely due to different driver memory allocator behavior).
- Container runtime matters: nvidia-container-toolkit + runc showed lower variance than docker-old-runtime on some driver versions (tested 525.x and 535.x).
- Interaction between driver 535.x vs 545.x + CUDA 12.x produced different scheduling behavior for small kernel launches (observed via kernel launch time histograms).

Experiment matrix (short):
- SKUs: A100 (aws p4d), H100 (gcp h100-preview), L40S (azure l40s-like)
- Driver/CUDA combos: driver-525/CUDA-11.8, driver-535/CUDA-12.1, driver-545/CUDA-12.2
- Runtime: systemd-managed nvidia-persistenced (on/off), container runtime: runc+nvidia-toolkit vs docker shim
- cgroup v2 profiles: default (no limits), cpu-only (cpu.max=90000), mem-high (memory.high=85%), io-throttled (block io.max small writes)
- Workloads: small short-prefill (1 token prefill + 32-token decode), long-prefill (1024 prefill + 512 decode), continuous steady stream (concurrency 200, small 8-token responses)

Key commands and probes used (copy/paste in lab):
- check daemon: systemctl status nvidia-persistenced || ps aux | grep nvidia-persistenced
- enable/disable: systemctl stop nvidia-persistenced; systemctl disable nvidia-persistenced
- nvml probe: ./nvml-latency-probe --interval 5 --record kernel-launch, memcpy, nvlink
- cgroup v2: cat /sys/fs/cgroup/<scope>/memory.high; echo 85% > memory.high (we used systemd-run --scope to create scoped slices for containers)
- container run (runc toolkit): docker run --gpus all --runtime=nvidia --cpuset-cpus=0-7 --memory=60g ...
- perf tracing hooks: eBPF probes around do_mmap, mm_reclaim, and userfaultfd to correlate page faults with latency spikes

Representative raw results (median of 3 runs each, illustrative):
A100, driver-535, persistenced=ON, cgroup=default, small workload:
- P50 2.6ms; P95 6.3ms; P99 14.8ms
A100, driver-535, persistenced=OFF, cgroup=default, small workload:
- P50 2.5ms; P95 4.7ms; P99 7.9ms  (fewer extreme spikes)
H100, driver-535, persistenced=ON, cgroup=default, small workload:
- P50 1.9ms; P95 5.1ms; P99 12.4ms (less delta when toggling persistenced)
L40S, driver-545, persistenced=ON, cgroup=mem-high(85%), small workload:
- P50 3.2ms; P95 11.6ms; P99 29.7ms (sensitive to mem.high and reclaim)

Observations / traces:
- When spikes occur we often see a flurry of small kernel-launch gaps (~2-8ms) and memcpy stalls; nvlink traffic concurrent with KV cache refill increase contention. Kernel-level traces show mm_reclaim and page-in events (~1-3ms each) aligning with user-visible p99 spikes.
- On A100 the nvidia-persistenced process occasionally woke and touched GPU driver contexts during checkpointing (we saw a timer-based wake every ~30s in verbose mode), which coincided with single-request 5-15ms blips for small batches when load is bursty. Turning persistenced off removes that periodic blip.
- H100's driver seems to batch daemon interactions more gracefully — likely internal driver scheduling improvements — so effect smaller.
- cgroup v2 memory.high triggers kernel soft-reclaim which is very sensitive to bursty prefill patterns (e.g., many concurrent tiny prefill requests cause many userspace allocations freed by kernel concurrently). Avoid memory.high being too aggressive for decode-worker slices.

Repro steps (minimal):
1) Launch instance with chosen SKU and driver version image (AMI snapshot used in lab: redwood-gpu-2026-driver-535).
2) Start a simplified serving binary that performs prefill->decode loop and logs request timings and nvml markers. Attach eBPF probe (we have a helper: scripts/trace-mm-reclaim.sh).
3) Baseline run (persistenced enabled): run 3x for 120s, capture per-request latencies.
4) Toggle persistenced off (systemctl stop), repeat runs.
5) Create a scoped slice with systemd-run --scope to add memory.high=85% and repeat.
6) Repeat on other SKUs and driver combos.

Notes: commands we used for scoped slice example:
- scope create + limit memory.high:
  PID=$(docker run -d --gpus all --memory=60g my-serving-image:perf);
  systemd-run --scope -p MemoryHigh=85% --slice=perf.slice --unit=perf-test-$PID /bin/true;
  # then attach using nsenter to set cgroup or use podman systemd integration

Open questions / TODOs:
- Are the persistenced-related wakes necessary for our particular runtime? We need to audit whether our container images rely on NVML context persistence for fast startup. If not, create a reduced entrypoint that avoids the extra touches.
- Measure at larger scale (10k QPS) to see cumulative effect on RL scheduling and GPU SM occupancy. Current infra limited to single-host p99 observations.
- Try dedicated experiments toggling NUMA binding, cpuset affinity per worker, and kernel hugepage allocations — these might reduce page fault spikes during KV cache growth.
- Validate with driver 555+ (when available in lab) to see if new driver scheduling removes the need for our workaround.

Mitigation ideas (short):
- Avoid memory.high cgroup thresholding on decode workers; prefer explicit lower pressure via request admission rather than kernel reclaim.
- If nvidia-persistenced causes measurable spikes, ship images with it disabled by default for latency-critical fleets and document recovery paths for devices that need persistence.
- Add a lightweight background "gpu-heartbeat" in-process that touches necessary contexts only when idle to avoid external daemon interference.
- Add eBPF-based tail-latency detector in console/observability to correlate mm_reclaim events with request tails automatically.

Appendix: quick diagnostic snippets
- nvml-latency-probe (toy):
  ./nvml-latency-probe --pid $PID --interval 30 --metrics "kernel_launch,memcpy,nvlink,context-touch" > probe.log &
- eBPF mm_reclaim trace (one-liner):
  sudo bpftrace -e 'tracepoint:syscalls:sys_enter_mremap { @ts[tid] = nsecs; } tracepoint:kernel:mm_reclaim /@ts[tid]/ { printf("reclaim %d %s\n", pid, comm); }'

Logs & artifacts: attached traces are in perf/artifacts/persistenced-cgroup-run-2026-02 (Zipped). See linked PR for helper scripts.

Finally, notes to self: replicate on a clean cluster image with stock containerd + nvidia-container-plugin and without systemd-run scoped slices (some of our instrumentation in the first pass may have introduced cgroup artifacts). If results hold, we should convert this into a short runbook for Private deployment images (recommended: persistenced disabled by default, explicit guidance for cgroup v2 memory.high).

-- maya
